planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts once nights stay above 50F; mulch roots heavily where winter lows approach the mid-20s.

directions: Plant in loamy, well-drained soil enriched with compost, choosing a site with morning sun and afternoon shade in the Gulf Coast heat. Water regularly until established, then taper to moderate watering since the shrub tolerates short dry spells once rooted. Shear back hard after the main fall-to-spring bloom flush to keep growth dense and to encourage the next wave of violet-blue flowers. In zone 9, expect the top growth to die back after a hard freeze; it typically resprouts from the base in spring.

planting.note: Move containerized plants outdoors after all frost danger passes; this species is slower to recover from cold than its yellow-flowered relative.

directions: Site this upright tropical shrub where it gets bright filtered light or a few hours of morning sun with afternoon shade, since strong midday sun can scorch the broad leaves in Gulf Coast summers. Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, working in compost at planting to hold moisture around the shallow root zone. Pinch young stems to encourage branching, as unpruned plants grow tall and leggy while still producing their showy red bracted flower spikes. Where winters dip into the 20s, treat as a cut-back perennial and mulch the crown heavily for regrowth from the roots.

planting.note: Set out divisions or rooted stem cuttings once soil has warmed; this low grower fills in quickly along shaded bed edges.

directions: Grow this low mounding groundcover in filtered light to partial shade, which keeps the cream-and-green marbled leaves from bleaching out in strong sun. Provide evenly moist, well-drained soil and pinch stem tips regularly to keep the habit compact and bushy rather than sprawling. Small tubular pink-violet flowers appear intermittently among the foliage, but the plant is grown primarily for its variegated leaf color along shaded borders and containers. Take stem cuttings before the first fall frost to overwinter indoors, since top growth is killed by even light freezes.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Best established from nursery-grown starts or cuttings in spring; direct seed is slow and erratic.

directions: Plant this low Texas-native subshrub in part sun to dappled shade on well-drained, often rocky or limestone-based soil, mimicking its natural woodland-edge habitat. Water it in to establish, then let it dry between waterings, since it handles heat and drought well once rooted. It produces small cream flowers marked with pink or purple from late summer through spring, making it a valuable off-season nectar source in a native pollinator bed. Cut back old growth in late winter to refresh the clump before the next bloom cycle begins.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database
